questions.q: What does each `RUN`, `COPY`, or `ADD` instruction in a Dockerfile produce?
options: A separate, unrelated image
Its own filesystem layer, stacked on top of the layer produced by the previous instruction
A new container, independent of the build
Nothing on disk -- those instructions only affect runtime behavior
questions.explain: Each of these instructions creates a new layer -- a filesystem diff -- stacked on the layers before it, which is also the unit Docker's build cache operates on.

questions.q: In the Northbridge build where only `server.js` changed (not `package.json`), why did the `RUN npm install` step show as `CACHED`?
options: Because npm install always shows as cached regardless of changes
Because that layer's instruction and inputs (package.json, package-lock.json) hadn't changed since the last build, so Docker reused the previously built layer
Because the internet connection was down during the build
Because CACHED only means the step was skipped entirely with no output image
questions.explain: Docker's build cache keys each layer on its instruction plus its inputs. Since package.json and package-lock.json were unchanged, Docker safely reused the existing npm install layer.

questions.q: If `package.json` changes, what happens to the `COPY . .` layer that comes after it, even though the application code itself didn't change?
options: It stays cached because its own inputs didn't change
It gets rebuilt anyway, because every layer after an invalidated layer is rebuilt regardless of whether its own inputs changed
Docker skips it and reuses the oldest available version
The build fails until the code is also changed
questions.explain: Layer caching is sequential: once one layer must rebuild, every layer stacked after it rebuilds too, even if that specific layer's own inputs are unchanged.

questions.q: Why does the Northbridge Dockerfile copy `package.json` and run `npm install` before copying the rest of the application code?
options: Dockerfile syntax requires dependency files to be copied before any other files
Because package.json changes rarely while application code changes constantly -- ordering this way keeps the expensive install step cached through most code edits
It makes no difference to build speed, only to final image size
npm install cannot run after any other COPY instruction
questions.explain: Placing the rarely-changing dependency install before the frequently-changing code copy maximizes cache hits, since invalidating a layer forces every later layer to rebuild.

questions.q: If the Dockerfile instead did `COPY . .` before `RUN npm install`, what would happen on every single code edit?
options: Nothing would change -- the build would still be fast
Every code edit would invalidate the COPY layer and force npm install to rerun from scratch every time, since it comes after
The build would fail immediately
Docker would automatically reorder the instructions for you
questions.explain: With COPY . . first, any code change invalidates that layer -- and since npm install comes after it, that slow step would rerun on every build instead of staying cached.
